questions.q: What is the difference between latency and throughput?
options: They are two names for the same measurement
Latency is the time for one request to complete; throughput is how many requests a system can process per unit time
Latency measures requests per second; throughput measures milliseconds per request
Latency only applies to databases, throughput only applies to web servers
questions.explain: Latency is about one request's end-to-end wait time, while throughput is about overall capacity — how many requests the system handles in a given time window.

questions.q: Why can batching requests together increase throughput while also increasing latency?
options: Batching has no effect on either metric
Processing in bulk is more efficient and raises throughput, but individual requests now wait for the batch to fill, raising their latency
Batching only affects throughput, never latency
Batching eliminates network hops entirely
questions.explain: Batching improves overall efficiency (throughput) but makes individual requests wait longer before being processed (higher latency) — a direct tradeoff.

questions.q: Why does p99 latency matter more than average latency in a distributed system where one request fans out to many downstream services?
options: Because the overall response can only be as fast as the slowest downstream call, so a single slow dependency can affect a large share of requests even if it's rarely slow on its own
Because p99 is always a smaller number than the average
Because average latency is not a real statistical measurement
Because p99 only applies to single-machine programs
questions.explain: When a request depends on many downstream calls, the total time is bounded by the slowest one. Even a dependency that's slow only 1% of the time can drag down a meaningful share of overall requests across many calls.

questions.q: Why does a request that fans out to five downstream services in a distributed system take on latency that a single-machine program never had?
options: Because each of the five calls crosses a network and pays a real round-trip travel cost that a local function call doesn't
Because distributed systems always use slower CPUs
Because five services always process data less efficiently than one
Because network hops only affect throughput, not latency
questions.explain: On a single machine, a function call is effectively instant. Once a request has to cross the network to call another machine, that trip adds real travel time — and each additional hop adds more.

questions.q: A background data-processing job and a live user-facing checkout page have different priorities. Which pairing best reflects the tradeoff covered in this lesson?
options: The background job should favor low latency; the checkout page should favor high throughput
The background job should favor high throughput; the checkout page should favor low latency
Both should favor throughput exclusively
Both should favor latency exclusively, since throughput never matters
questions.explain: Bulk background processing benefits from maximizing throughput even if individual items take longer, while a live, interactive user flow needs each request to feel fast — favoring low latency.
